title: Mathematics
source: Generated from “Timeline of mathematics” on Wikipedia; each event links to its source article.

events.title: Zhoubi Suanjing
events.text: 1046 BC to 256 BC – China, Zhoubi Suanjing, arithmetic, geometric algorithms, and proofs.

events.title: combinatorial
events.text: The earliest recorded use of combinatorial techniques comes from problem 79 of the Rhind papyrus, which dates to the 16th century BCE.

events.title: Plato
events.text: 347 BC – Greece, Plato

events.title: Aristarchus of Samos
events.text: 230 BC – Greece, Aristarchus of Samos

events.title: Apollonius of Perga
events.text: Greece, Apollonius of Perga writes On Conic Sections and names the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.

events.title: Liu Xin
events.text: 23 AD – China, Liu Xin

events.title: zero
events.text: the earliest known use of zero as a decimal digit is introduced by Indian mathematicians.

events.title: Varāhamihira
events.text: 587—India, Varāhamihira

events.title: Abu Kamil
events.text: c. 900—Egypt, Abu Kamil had begun to understand what we would write in symbols as <math>x^n \cdot x^m = x^{m+n}</math>

events.title: Omar Khayyam
events.text: Omar Khayyam begins to write Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra and classifies cubic equations.

events.title: 1427—Jamshid al-Kashi completes The Key to Arithmetic, containing work
events.text: 1427—Jamshid al-Kashi completes The Key to Arithmetic, containing work of great depth on decimal fractions. It applies arithmetical and algebraic methods to the solution of various problems, including several geometric ones.

events.title: Ludolph van Ceulen
events.text: 1596—Ludolph van Ceulen computes π to twenty decimal places using inscribed and circumscribed polygons.

events.title: Christopher Wren
events.text: 1658—Christopher Wren shows that the length of a cycloid is four times the diameter of its generating circle.

events.title: Abraham Sharp
events.text: 1699—Abraham Sharp calculates π to 72 digits, but only 71 are correct.

events.title: Jean le Rond d'Alembert
events.text: 1747—Jean le Rond d'Alembert solves the vibrating string problem (one-dimensional wave equation).

events.title: Louis Poinsot
events.text: 1806—Louis Poinsot discovers the two remaining Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra.

events.title: János Bolyai
events.text: János Bolyai, Gauss, and Lobachevsky invent hyperbolic non-Euclidean geometry.

events.title: George Gabriel Stokes rediscovers and proves Stokes' theorem
events.text: George Gabriel Stokes rediscovers and proves Stokes' theorem.

events.title: Sophus Lie
events.text: Sophus Lie publishes work on transformation groups, serving as the foundation for the modern theory of Lie groups.

events.title: Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer
events.text: Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer presents the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.

events.title: Tadeusz Banachiewicz
events.text: Tadeusz Banachiewicz introduces LU decomposition.

events.title: John Wrench
events.text: John Wrench and L. R. Smith compute π to 2,037 decimal places using ENIAC.

events.title: John G. F. Francis
events.text: John G. F. Francis and Vera Kublanovskaya independently develop the QR algorithm to calculate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix.

events.title: Pierre Deligne
events.text: Pierre Deligne solves the last and deepest of the Weil conjectures, completing the program of Grothendieck.

events.title: Thomas Callister Hales
events.text: Thomas Callister Hales (almost certainly) proves the Kepler conjecture.

events.title: Aaron Naber
events.text: Elia Bruè, Aaron Naber, and Daniele Semola disprove the Milnor conjecture for six or more dimensions.
